title: Born And Raised

jokes.text: Sweetums Cares, a non-profit group, that puts umbrella hats on homeless people when it rains.
jokes.setup: A radio sponsorship read — a mundane, corporate-sounding charity name 'Sweetums Cares'
jokes.punchline: The charity's mission is the utterly ridiculous and specific act of putting umbrella hats on homeless people when it rains — framed with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A perfect cold-open absurdist joke. The specificity of 'umbrella hats' is what elevates it — not just charity, not just hats, but umbrella hats, and only when it rains. The deadpan delivery of a genuine non-profit mission makes it land. Strong originality and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Announcer
dialogue.line: This message brought to you by the Pawnee Chamber of Commerce. We're committed to helping those in need. That's why we've donated over 10,000 umbrella hats to homeless people in our community.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Announcer
dialogue.line: Because nothing says 'we care' like a hat that's also an umbrella. Specifically designed so homeless people can stay dry while remaining completely unable to use their hands.

jokes.text: David Parker, who took off for eight months to study the migration patterns of our nation's squirrels. We have not seen him since.
jokes.setup: Standard radio host intro explaining a fill-in host
jokes.punchline: 'We have not seen him since' — delivered as a throwaway afterthought, implying the squirrel researcher may be dead or missing
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly economical dark joke. The structure is perfect: establish the absurd premise (squirrel migration study), then the punchline lands with maximum brevity. 'We have not seen him since' does enormous work in six words. The nonchalant tone is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Derry Murbles
dialogue.line: We'll be back after these messages. I'm taking a vacation to study the squirrel migration patterns in the greater Pawnee area.

dialogue.speaker: Derry Murbles
dialogue.line: My research assistant Gary was supposed to join me, but I haven't seen him since we entered the woods three days ago.

jokes.text: Leslie, could one say that a book is nothing more than a painting of words, which are the notes on the tapestry of the greatest film ever sculpted?
jokes.setup: A radio interview question about Leslie's book — should be a simple journalistic question
jokes.punchline: Murbles delivers an utterly nonsensical, word-salad pseudo-intellectual metaphor that mixes multiple art forms incoherently ('sculpted' a film, 'notes on a tapestry')
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. Murbles is a perfect parody of pretentious public radio hosts, and the joke works on multiple levels: the mixed metaphors escalate absurdly, the question is unanswerable, and it's deeply specific to this character. 'The greatest film ever sculpted' is a genuinely brilliant non-sequitur. Earns its 8+ score through originality and perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was editing the Pawnee Historical Society's guide, and I found some really inappropriate content that had to be removed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: There was this whole section I wrote about how Tom Haverford's great-great-grandfather was a suspected horse thief, and I may have added some editorial commentary about how 'the apple doesn't fall far from the tree.'

jokes.text: One could say that. But should one?
jokes.setup: Murbles asks his absurd question about books being 'paintings of words'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's perfectly composed, diplomatic non-answer that gently signals the question was idiotic without being rude
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. Maximum economy — five words that do everything. It's quintessential Leslie: she's diplomatic, she won't insult the host, but she can't help letting her intelligence peek through. The parallel structure ('One could say... But should one?') is elegant and highly quotable. Easily earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Derry Murbles
dialogue.line: You see, the brushstrokes of Monet are like the percussion section of a Debussy composition—both are essentially sandwiches.

jokes.text: Join us next week when David Bianculli will be filling in for Richard Chang-Jefferson, who will be filling in for me.
jokes.setup: Standard radio sign-off mentioning next week's host
jokes.punchline: Murbles reveals a recursive chain of fill-ins — filling in for the fill-in for himself — implying the station is in total organizational chaos
jokes.explanation: A good absurdist escalation on the running gag of the station's chaos. The recursive structure is clever — Murbles is filling in for someone, and now he needs someone to fill in for him. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's a great question, and I appreciate you asking it, but I'm going to stop you right there because I have no idea what you just said.

jokes.text: Please enjoy a song from the lesbian Afro-Norwegian funk duo, Nefertiti's Fjord.
jokes.setup: Standard radio sign-off: 'Please enjoy a song from...'
jokes.punchline: The band is described with an escalating cascade of specific identity modifiers — lesbian, Afro-Norwegian, funk duo — culminating in the absurd band name 'Nefertiti's Fjord'
jokes.explanation: A standout joke. The comedy builds through specificity — each modifier ('lesbian,' 'Afro-Norwegian,' 'funk') is funnier than the last, and 'Nefertiti's Fjord' as the name is a masterpiece of absurdist comedy writing. It sounds like exactly what a pretentious public radio station would play. The band name alone is quotable. High originality.

jokes.text: Oh, wow. They are terrible. / Yes, they're quite awful, but they are lesbians. So...
jokes.setup: They listen to Nefertiti's Fjord playing
jokes.punchline: Murbles acknowledges the music is awful but defends it on identity grounds alone ('they are lesbians. So...') — a skewering of performative progressivism
jokes.explanation: The callback landing makes this a gem. 'They are lesbians. So...' with the trailing off is perfect — Murbles doesn't even finish the justification because there isn't one. The trailing 'So...' does all the work. Sharp social satire delivered with total deadpan sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know this music is terrible, but we have to support local artists.

dialogue.speaker: Derry Murbles
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's just a guy playing a kazoo in the corner.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A LOCAL guy playing a kazoo in the corner.

jokes.text: Usually, I only read nautical novels and my own personal manifestos, but I'm proud to make this exception.
jokes.setup: Ron is presenting Leslie with a signed copy of her book as a gift
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals his reading list — 'nautical novels and my own personal manifestos' — character-specific absurdist detail that perfectly encapsulates Ron
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson. 'Nautical novels and my own personal manifestos' is one of the best character-specific jokes in the episode. It works because both elements are deeply Ron: nautical novels speak to his rugged self-sufficiency aesthetic, and 'my own personal manifestos' suggests he has written multiple screeds that he re-reads for pleasure. Maximum character integration. Earns its 8+ comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have made an exception and read your book.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really? What did you think?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It was well-written. Engaging. I read it in one sitting.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's wonderful!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was in the bathtub. Naked. For seven hours.

jokes.text: God, this goes on for, like, seven pages. I started thinking about you as a woman and as a person, and I got carried away.
jokes.setup: Leslie hands out signed copies of her book; a recipient notices their inscription is unusually long
jokes.punchline: Leslie admits she wrote a seven-page personal inscription because she 'got carried away' thinking about the recipient as a woman and a person — her enthusiasm overrides all normal boundaries
jokes.explanation: Strong Leslie Knope character comedy. Her inability to be brief or restrained when she cares about someone is a core character trait, and 'I started thinking about you as a woman and as a person' is a funny escalation — the phrase sounds therapeutic and slightly unhinged. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I wanted to make sure it was comprehensive. I included all of my accomplishments, my philosophy on public service, and a detailed timeline of the Pawnee Parks Department's greatest achievements.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's a plaque.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know that, Ben. But I also wanted to make it personal. So I added some reflections on what this job has meant to me, how it's shaped who I am, and how grateful I am for everyone who's supported me along the way.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, but the part that concerns me is where you wrote, 'I will never stop thinking about this job. It consumes my every waking moment. I dream about it at night.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What's wrong with that?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It sounds like you're in love with the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I AM in love with the Parks Department!

jokes.text: Okay, mine just says, 'Get well soon.' / Aren't you sick? / No. / Something's off.
jokes.setup: After hearing about the seven-page inscription, Ben reveals his copy has a perfunctory 'Get well soon' inscription
jokes.punchline: The recipient is not sick, revealing Leslie's inscription was either inattentive or a weird habit — 'Something's off' is Ben's understated concern
jokes.explanation: A nice quick beat that inverts the previous joke. Where one inscription was comically excessive, Ben's is bizarrely minimal and wrong. The triple beat — 'Get well soon' / 'Aren't you sick?' / 'No' / 'Something's off' — is efficient comedy construction.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You son of a bitch.

jokes.text: I loved your book. I read it cover to cover. / I just gave it to you an hour ago. / I'm a speed reader. I can read over 3,000 words a minute, with total comprehension. One time, I read all of Siddhartha at a traffic stop.
jokes.setup: Chris compliments Leslie's book effusively and claims to have read it all
jokes.punchline: Chris's manic over-achievement extends to reading — 3,000 words per minute is absurd enough, but 'total comprehension' and 'read all of Siddhartha at a traffic stop' escalates it perfectly
jokes.explanation: Classic Chris Traeger character comedy. His superhuman positivity and performance-anxiety extends to reading speed. 'With total comprehension' is a great specificity addition — people who make false claims always over-specify. 'Siddhartha at a traffic stop' is a perfect escalating punchline: the book choice is pretentious, the location is mundane, the claim is absurd.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm a speed reader. I can read 20,000 words per minute.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, that's not possible.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I read the entire traffic code once. Got pulled over for speeding. Cop said I was going 150 in a 35. I told him I was just speed reading the road signs.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Did it work?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No. He gave me a ticket for speeding and one for reckless endangerment.

jokes.text: Pawnee's most notorious businessman in the building. I brought some Entertainment 720 pillowcases for your pillow. Never Stop Dreaming. Tom Haverford.
jokes.setup: Tom arrives at a book event
jokes.punchline: Tom introduces himself in the third person and has branded pillowcases that say 'Never Stop Dreaming. Tom Haverford.' — absurdly grandiose self-promotion for a failing business
jokes.explanation: Very Tom Haverford — the branding of everything, the third-person self-reference, the inspirational motto. The pillowcases are a specifically absurd merch choice. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I made promotional pillowcases for the Parks Department. Check it out.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Tom, this pillowcase has a picture of a sewage treatment plant on it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I thought it really captures the essence of what we do here.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I appreciate the effort, Tom, I really do. But I'm not sure people want to rest their heads on a picture of raw sewage.

jokes.text: I never do. Chris Traeger. / Respect. Game recognize game.
jokes.setup: Tom's pillowcase says 'Never Stop Dreaming'; Chris responds
jokes.punchline: Chris takes the slogan literally/sincerely while Tom responds with 'Game recognize game' — Tom treating the exchange as two power players recognizing each other, when Chris is being earnest
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional character beat. Chris's sincerity vs. Tom's bravado is a reliable dynamic. 'Game recognize game' in this context is funny but not exceptional.

jokes.text: The Time-Traveler's Optometrist, by Pawnee's own Penelope Foster. A heartwarming story about a caveman eye doctor who travels to present-day Cincinnati and can see everything but love. Unreadable.
jokes.setup: Tom explains the power of Joan's Book Club sticker by describing a previous selection
jokes.punchline: The book description escalates absurdly ('caveman eye doctor,' 'present-day Cincinnati,' 'can see everything but love') and then Tom delivers the flat verdict: 'Unreadable.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The book description is a masterwork of absurdist escalation: 'caveman' plus 'optometrist' is already funny, then 'present-day Cincinnati' is a hilariously unambitious destination, then 'can see everything but love' is a perfect parody of sentimental taglines. Then 'Unreadable.' punctures it all with deadpan economy. Every word earns its place. The joke also works structurally as a parody of bad literary fiction. Clearly earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: "From the moment I picked your book up until I laid it down, I was convulsed with laughter. Some day I hope to read it." - Groucho Marx

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But you know what? Joan from accounting put this five-star review on Amazon, and now it's a bestseller.

jokes.text: I think she wants one of her big 'gotcha' moments. / Well, she's not going to 'getch' me.
jokes.setup: Tom warns Leslie that Joan might spring a 'gotcha' on her
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defensive response accidentally mangles 'gotcha' into 'getch me' — her determination creates a verbal stumble
jokes.explanation: A small but charming Leslie moment. The accidental verbal fumble 'getch' in a moment of bravado is very character-specific — Leslie is smart but her passion overrides her precision. Quick and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Joan Callamezzo has these 'gotcha' moments where she tries to trip you up.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not going to fall for it. I'm prepared for anything she throws at me. Bring it on, Joan. I welcome the challenge. I'm not afraid.

jokes.text: I doubt it. If there's one thing Leslie's not, it's sloppy. She's also not brief. This is going to take forever.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if there's really a mistake in Leslie's book
jokes.punchline: The defense of Leslie pivots into a deadpan complaint about the book's length — 'She's also not brief. This is going to take forever.'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed talking-head beat. The pivot from compliment ('not sloppy') to complaint ('not brief') is a classic misdirection structure — you expect continued praise, get a groan instead. Character-consistent with the established joke about Leslie's verbosity.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, Leslie makes mistakes like everyone else, but her thoroughness is actually her greatest strength.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: So... you're saying she's thorough?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's not a compliment, Ben. That's what we say about people we don't like.

jokes.text: It's just us, I hope. / I wish. / Hey, guys. Ready to do some fact-checking? / Here we go. Helping Leslie.
jokes.setup: Ben and April are apparently hoping for a quiet work session
jokes.punchline: Chris cheerfully bursts in, oblivious to their mutual reluctance; April's deadpan 'Here we go. Helping Leslie.' captures shared suffering
jokes.explanation: A functional scene-setting joke. April's monotone 'Here we go. Helping Leslie.' is quintessential April — she delivers enthusiasm as if reading from a script of someone else's enthusiasm. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why are all these people here?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't know. I guess they heard we needed help.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, tell them to leave.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't want to hurt their feelings.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I do.

jokes.text: At the risk of bragging, one of the things I'm best at is riding coattails. Behind every successful man, is me, smiling and taking partial credit.
jokes.setup: Tom explains his business strategy for leveraging Leslie's book success
jokes.punchline: Tom openly and proudly declares his parasitic business model — 'riding coattails' and 'taking partial credit' — as if these are admirable skills
jokes.explanation: A standout Tom Haverford talking-head. The joke works because he frames cowardly opportunism as a genuine skill and brags about it. 'At the risk of bragging' signals self-awareness that is immediately undercut. 'Behind every successful man, is me, smiling and taking partial credit' is highly quotable and a perfectly constructed inversion of the 'behind every successful man' cliché. Earns 8+ through originality, character integration, and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Joan, we've actually met before. Remember? At the city council meeting last month?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I have no idea who you are.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But you were sitting right next to me. We talked for twenty minutes about zoning regulations.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Doesn't ring a bell.

jokes.text: Wow, you guys are really cute together. / Ben, I'm cute together with everybody.
jokes.setup: Someone comments that Joan and Ben look cute together
jokes.punchline: Joan corrects the assumption — not that she and Ben are special, but that she is universally cute with everyone, an expression of total narcissism
jokes.explanation: A quick, sharp character joke for Joan. The correction is the joke — she doesn't deny being cute, she just expands the claim universally. Efficient and character-revealing.

jokes.text: Anyone find any mistakes? / Yeah, actually, in here it says that Pawnee is great. But in reality, it's terrible.
jokes.setup: Tom asks if anyone found factual errors in the book
jokes.punchline: April's 'mistake' is not a factual error but her personal opinion — delivered with complete deadpan sincerity
jokes.explanation: A very April joke. She responds to a factual question with her nihilistic opinion, treating her pessimism as objective error-correction. Perfect economy — two sentences that reveal everything about her character. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm a parasite. I feed off the success of others and I'm very good at it.

jokes.text: Hey, I'm thinking about getting a new phone. Do you guys like your phones? / I've never used a phone in my life.
jokes.setup: Chris tries to make small talk with Ron and April by asking about phones
jokes.punchline: Ron declares he has never used a phone in his life — an absurd claim that is also completely plausible for Ron Swanson
jokes.explanation: A great Ron Swanson joke. The claim is so extreme it circles back to being completely believable for this character. Maximum economy: six words that are both absurdist and character-defining. Ron's anti-technology, anti-government philosophy makes this feel earned rather than random.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Of course we do. I'm adorable and he has the good sense to stand next to me.

jokes.text: What about you, Ron? Do you like your phone? / Mmm.
jokes.setup: Chris follows up specifically asking Ron about his phone
jokes.punchline: Ron's entire response is a noncommittal grunt — 'Mmm.' — which functions as the joke because it's his complete dismissal of Chris's attempt at connection
jokes.explanation: The single syllable response is very Ron, and works well after the previous joke. Maximum economy (literally one syllable) but limited quotability outside context.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, there's a huge factual error in your book. You say that the government exists to serve the people. That's not true. The government exists to take our money and tell us what to do.

jokes.text: Here's my goal. I'm going to get these two people that I've known for a long time to talk to me for five minutes. Who am I kidding? One minute. One minute would be amazing.
jokes.setup: Chris talking-head about his social ambitions for the day
jokes.punchline: Chris's goal — usually absurdly high — is comically modest here: five minutes of small talk, then revised down to one minute, which he treats as 'amazing'
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. Chris is perpetually optimistic and high-achieving, so watching him lower his bar in real-time to desperate levels is a nice inversion. The self-correction from five minutes to one is the key structural move.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no use for a phone. I don't want people calling me, and I certainly don't want to call them.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If something is important, they can find me in person. If it's not important, I don't care about it.

jokes.text: We received a tip that you, Leslie 'Born and Raised' Knope, were not born in Pawnee. / Gotcha!
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to get the book club sticker applied to her book on live TV
jokes.punchline: Joan springs the bombshell accusation with 'Gotcha!' — the word she's been building toward, now deployed at maximum theatrical impact
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the episode's A-plot setup. Joan's theatricality as a local TV journalist is perfectly captured. The callback to Leslie's 'she's not going to getch me' makes it a satisfying structural payoff. High impact as a plot-driving comedic reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have really high standards when it comes to dating. A woman has to be intelligent, beautiful, independent... Actually, no. A woman just has to talk to me. That's it. That's the bar. If a woman has ever spoken words in my direction, I'm convinced we're soulmates.

jokes.text: I have to tell you. This feels like 'Gotcha' journalism. / In what way? / That way. You put 'Gotcha' on my face.
jokes.setup: Leslie objects to Joan's journalism tactics
jokes.punchline: Leslie accuses Joan of 'Gotcha journalism' — and Joan's literal 'Gotcha' stamp/graphic has apparently been placed on Leslie's face, making Leslie's critique literally accurate in the most absurd way
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly constructed visual/verbal joke. 'Gotcha journalism' is a serious media criticism term; here it's literalized because Joan's graphic actually stamps 'Gotcha' on Leslie's face. The verbal and visual pun work simultaneously. 'That way. You put Gotcha on my face.' is a perfect punchline — specific, visual, and the explanation makes it funnier. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: You want this book club sticker?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! Please, I need it for my binder!

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Too bad.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: *lunges desperately* Come on, Joan! *falls over* Please! *crawls* I'm begging you!

jokes.text: Where was Leslie Knope actually born? Pawnee. We will pull out the world map and speculate wildly.
jokes.setup: Joan teases the post-break segment about Leslie's birthplace
jokes.punchline: The answer is stated immediately ('Pawnee') and then immediately contradicted by promising to 'speculate wildly' with a world map — local TV news inflating a non-story to maximum drama
jokes.explanation: Sharp media satire. The joke captures local TV news perfectly — stating the obvious answer and then promising unnecessary dramatic speculation anyway. 'Speculate wildly' is a great phrase that parodies breathless TV journalism.

jokes.text: Oh, God. Not the 'Gotcha' dancers.
jokes.setup: Joan's show cuts to a break featuring what are apparently regular 'Gotcha' dancers
jokes.punchline: Ben's resigned groan implies he's seen the Gotcha dancers before — they are a recurring and deeply embarrassing fixture of Joan's show
jokes.explanation: The implication that Joan has a dedicated team of 'Gotcha' dancers on standby is a brilliant piece of worldbuilding comedy. Ben's weary recognition sells it — this is apparently not their first rodeo. The visual of actual dancers performing to a 'Gotcha' theme is inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe they used gotcha journalism on me. That's so unfair and unethical.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Well, look on the bright side.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What bright side? My reputation is ruined!

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: At least you got a cool graphic out of it.

jokes.text: That was despicable I am horrified at her tactics. That said, the show was very lively. / Joan 'Gotcha' Don't it hurt ya / It's pretty catchy.
jokes.setup: Leslie morally objects to Joan's ambush journalism; the Gotcha song plays in the background
jokes.punchline: Both Leslie and Ben, despite their moral objections, are unable to deny that the show was entertaining and the jingle is catchy — their integrity is slightly undermined by their enjoyment
jokes.explanation: A good joke about human hypocrisy — moral outrage co-existing with genuine appreciation for the spectacle. The jingle 'Joan Gotcha Don't it hurt ya' being 'pretty catchy' is a nice deflating beat.

jokes.text: When Leslie's in trouble, there's only one man for the job. Bert Macklin, FBI. You thought I was dead? So did the President's enemies.
jokes.setup: The group is in crisis mode over Leslie's TV appearance
jokes.punchline: Andy breaks into his alter-ego FBI agent persona, Bert Macklin, and delivers a hard-boiled one-liner that implies he has previously faked his death in a presidential assassination conspiracy
jokes.explanation: Bert Macklin is a beloved Andy Dwyer bit, and 'You thought I was dead? So did the President's enemies.' is a perfect specimen. The line escalates from the absurd premise to an even more absurd implication that Bert has been involved in presidential-level intrigue. It's fully committed, quotable, and only Andy could deliver it. High character integration earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What are those dancers doing? That's not what we choreographed at all! This is a disaster!

jokes.text: All right, so, we don't have to fact check anymore. But Leslie wants us to be on 'Ready-Alert One' just in case something comes up. Now, I can get some real work done.
jokes.setup: The fact-checking assignment has been suspended
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'real work' clearly means doing nothing — his celebration of not working by 'getting real work done' is a perfect expression of his anti-government ethos
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson. His 'real work' is almost certainly not work at all — possibly woodworking, or just sitting. The joke is in the implication.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Joan, your journalism is irresponsible and dangerous. You're a menace to this community.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That said, that exposé on the mayor was absolutely riveting. I couldn't put it down.

jokes.text: You know, I think I'm just gonna hang out here with you guys, if that's cool. / It's not. / Great. I could leave. I could. But I'm not going to. I will get my one minute of small talk, damn it. And it will be casual and it will be amicable.
jokes.setup: Chris announces he'll join Ron and April despite their clear disinterest
jokes.punchline: April's flat 'It's not' is perfect, but Chris's complete refusal to take the hint — 'I could leave. I could. But I'm not going to' — and his self-motivating declaration about one minute of small talk escalates wonderfully
jokes.explanation: A great running bit paid off here. Chris's determination to achieve one minute of casual conversation — treated with the same intensity as a marathon — is a perfect character joke. April's 'It's not' is equally good. The escalation from 'if that's cool' to 'I will get my one minute, damn it' is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've been working on something. I call it 'Treat Yo Self: The Song.' It's catchy, it's got a good beat, and most importantly, it's a gotcha.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: ♪ Treat yo self, treat yo self, to the finer things in life. Treat yo self, treat yo self, like you're somebody's wife. ♪

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You see what I did there? It's self-aware, it's humorous, and it's going to be stuck in everyone's heads for days.

jokes.text: Sorry, Tom. I am first and foremost a journalist.
jokes.setup: Tom confronts Joan about the book club sticker after she ambushed Leslie
jokes.punchline: Joan claiming journalistic integrity immediately after a segment with 'Gotcha' dancers and a 'Gotcha' stamp on Leslie's face is peak irony
jokes.explanation: A functional irony joke — the claim of journalistic integrity is undercut by everything we've seen from Joan. Works because of context but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna help you out, Leslie. I'm gonna go deep undercover. My name is Agent Bert Macklin, FBI. I have no weaknesses. I can't be killed. And I will find your guy.

jokes.text: I think I speak on behalf of everyone in the entire world when I say, we need to know the truth about where you were born.
jokes.setup: A public forum about Leslie's book; someone asks about her birthplace
jokes.punchline: The grandiose claim that 'everyone in the entire world' cares about whether a small-town politician was born in county A or county B perfectly captures small-town pomposity
jokes.explanation: A decent observational joke about small-town self-importance. Functional but not particularly crafted — the joke is fairly obvious.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey guys, want to grab lunch? There's this great burger place downtown!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What about dinner then? Or breakfast? I make a mean scrambled egg.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Stop talking.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would rather eat a bowl of nails.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Cool, cool, cool. So Thursday?

jokes.text: No matter what you heard, ma'am, the truth is I was born here. / If you were so born here, then where's your birth certificate? / Well, I don't carry my birth certificate around with me. / Why? Because you're hiding something?
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to reason with an angry public forum attendee
jokes.punchline: The constituent's logic spirals into paranoid conspiracy — not having your birth certificate on your person equals hiding something
jokes.explanation: A good satirical beat about birthplace conspiracy theories and the impossible standard of proving a negative. The cringe of Leslie being unable to satisfy an irrational demand is effective.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We need Leslie back on Pawnee Today. She was the heart of this show.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I have an idea. What if we create a wall where all the people I've gotcha'd can come sign it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Jerry, that's... that's just a wall for your victims.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Exactly! It'll be iconic!

jokes.text: You should go back where you came from. / I am back from where I came from. / That sentence was confusing! You might as well be from China!
jokes.setup: An angry constituent tells Leslie to 'go back where she came from'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's perfectly logical response ('I am back from where I came from') confuses the constituent, who escalates to the non-sequitur accusation that she might as well be from China
jokes.explanation: A sharp satirical escalation. The logic trap Leslie creates is elegant — 'go back where you came from' fails when the person IS back there. The constituent's confusion escalating to 'you might as well be from China' is perfect absurdist xenophobia satire — the leap in logic mirrors how these arguments actually work. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben gave me some great business advice.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I just said 'don't spend more money than you make.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not advice, Tom. That's... that's just math.

jokes.text: When I was 18, Val Kilmer saw me at a mall and told me I should model. / That never happened.
jokes.setup: Joan begins a non-sequitur personal story apparently in the middle of an unrelated conversation (likely a confessional or aside)
jokes.punchline: A second voice (possibly Ben) flatly states 'That never happened' — the instant deflation of Joan's personal mythology
jokes.explanation: Three words that do everything. The setup (Val Kilmer spotted her at a mall) is already comic in its specificity and improbability, and 'That never happened' delivered flatly is the ideal punchline. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: She's been distant lately, but I've got a plan. I'm going to surprise her with a romantic dinner, really remind her why she fell for me in the first place.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mark my words, by the end of the night, she'll be signing papers.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Divorce papers.

jokes.text: So, Joan, how is married life treating you? / Santino and I are divorcing. Oh. It's actually quite liberating. I'm a woman with a strong sexual appetite. I'm like a caged peacock yearning for the wind on her haunches.
jokes.setup: Tom uses flattery about Joan's marriage as a seduction/manipulation tactic to get the book club sticker
jokes.punchline: Joan reveals she's divorcing, which Tom says 'Oh' to, and Joan then describes herself as 'a caged peacock yearning for the wind on her haunches' — an absurdly florid and specific metaphor for sexual desire
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'A caged peacock yearning for the wind on her haunches' is gloriously over-written, self-aggrandizing, and specific to the point of absurdity. It's exactly the kind of thing Joan would say. 'Haunches' is the key word — it takes the metaphor from pretentious to bizarre. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Audience Member
dialogue.line: So where was Leslie Knope born?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Pawnee, Indiana.

dialogue.speaker: Audience Member
dialogue.line: My God. Pawnee, Indiana produced Leslie Knope? That changes everything. That changes *everything*.

jokes.text: That's a powerful metaphor. / Maybe we can get that book club sticker in order, and we can work on unlocking that peacock cage.
jokes.setup: Joan has just described herself as a caged peacock
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately incorporates the peacock metaphor into his pitch — 'unlocking that peacock cage' — treating Joan's sexual metaphor as a business negotiation term
jokes.explanation: A well-executed callback. Tom using Joan's own flamboyant metaphor to make his pitch is a good cringe-comedy beat — he's trying to play her game but it's visibly awkward. Ben's flat 'That's a powerful metaphor' is also funny as an attempt to be diplomatic.

dialogue.speaker: Hostile audience member
dialogue.line: Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm from Eagleton.

dialogue.speaker: Hostile audience member
dialogue.line: No, where are you REALLY from?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Eagleton, Indiana. It's right next to Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Hostile audience member
dialogue.line: That's not a real place.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's definitely a real place. I grew up there.

dialogue.speaker: Hostile audience member
dialogue.line: Well, you sound foreign. Are you a citizen?

jokes.text: Things have changed, Tom. Don't make any promises you can't keep.
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching Joan on the book club sticker
jokes.punchline: Joan's sultry warning 'don't make any promises you can't keep' reframes the business negotiation as sexual foreplay — she's completely taken over the dynamic
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe beat that establishes Joan's dominance in the scene. The double entendre is functional but not especially crafted — the comedy comes more from the situation than the specific line.

dialogue.line: Unable to parse - insufficient context provided. The punchline text describing 'her immediate contradiction of her own lie' is not included. Please provide the actual dialogue text to parse.

jokes.text: I'll have another drink, and so will this adorable hunk of caramel to my right.
jokes.setup: Lunch with Joan, Tom, and Ben
jokes.punchline: Joan orders for Tom by calling him 'this adorable hunk of caramel' — objectifying, racialized, and completely inappropriate in the most Joan way possible
jokes.explanation: Joan at her most unhinged and inappropriate. 'Hunk of caramel' is a specific enough phrase to be genuinely funny — it's the kind of compliment that makes everyone uncomfortable, which is exactly the point. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I have the sexual appetite of a peacock. A peacock that just discovered cocaine.

jokes.text: Drink up, Tom. I'm going to go powder my nose. Amongst other things. If you know what I mean.
jokes.setup: Joan is about to leave the table
jokes.punchline: 'Powder my nose. Amongst other things. If you know what I mean.' — Joan's comically over-telegraphed implication makes it maximally uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: The triple escalation of the double entendre — 'powder my nose' → 'amongst other things' → 'if you know what I mean' — is funny because it over-explains the joke. Joan can't help herself.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm gonna say it. Ben, you're like a... you're like a wonderbread sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I... what?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Yeah. You're white, you're bland, and you get moldy if you don't use you right away.

jokes.text: Crap. / Is she going to powder her vagina?
jokes.setup: Joan leaves with her suggestive remark; Tom and Ben are left alone
jokes.punchline: Ben's question — completely sincere, completely horrified — literalizes Joan's implication in the most blunt possible way
jokes.explanation: Ben Wyatt saying this line is what makes it work — he's the straight man, the most normal person in the room, and this is his breaking point. The question is asked with complete sincerity and horror. 'Is she going to powder her vagina?' is shockingly direct in the most Ben Wyatt way possible, which makes it one of the episode's biggest laugh moments.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I'm going to powder my nose.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Your nose doesn't need powder. It looks fine. Are you having a skin condition? Because I know a dermatologist. Well, I know a guy who knows a dermatologist.

jokes.text: You've got to help me, man. / Why? Seems to be going the usual amount of gross.
jokes.setup: Tom is panicking about Joan's advances
jokes.punchline: Ben's assessment that this is 'the usual amount of gross' implies there is a baseline level of gross that is normal, and this has only reached that level
jokes.explanation: A good Ben Wyatt deadpan line. The idea that there is a normal baseline of grossness in their lives, and this only meets that threshold, is a well-constructed observational joke. 'The usual amount of gross' is a quotable phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, I know nerds. I am a nerd. And nerds are cool now. We run the world. We make the music, the movies, the TV shows. We invented the internet. We're not the weird kids anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And honestly, Tom, trying to be boring is actually way more embarrassing than just being yourself.

jokes.text: No, this is way different. She's not married anymore. She had, like, five bottles of alcohol. She's calling me 'caramel.'
jokes.setup: Tom escalating his case that this is worse than normal
jokes.punchline: The three-item list ends with 'She's calling me caramel' — which is the item he's most concerned about, delivered with maximum discomfort
jokes.explanation: A solid callback to the 'caramel' line. The list structure works well and 'she's calling me caramel' as the dealbreaker is funny — it's both the least and most threatening item on the list.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So April, what do you like to do for fun?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I like things.

jokes.text: You know, nerd culture is mainstream now. So, when you use the word 'nerd' derogatorily, it means you're the one that's out of the Zeitgeist. / Yes, that's perfect. Just like that. Be incredibly boring.
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ben to talk about 'nerd stuff' to cool down Joan's advances
jokes.punchline: Ben, told to talk about 'nerd stuff,' instead delivers a sociological defense of nerd culture — which Tom immediately identifies as 'incredibly boring' and therefore perfect
jokes.explanation: A great Ben Wyatt joke. He's asked to be boring, and instead of doing something performatively boring, he genuinely is boring in the most Ben way — a meta-defense of nerd culture using the word 'Zeitgeist.' Tom's immediate 'Yes, that's perfect. Just like that. Be incredibly boring' is a perfect straight-man response. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, your hair looks really nice today.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Thanks. I'm growing it out so I have something to hang myself with.

jokes.text: Well, I've made a little progress. I'm up to four seconds with April. / Hey, April. I was looking to get some new music. And I was wondering if you could recommend anything. / The Internet.
jokes.setup: Chris reports his small talk progress; then demonstrates by asking April for music recommendations
jokes.punchline: April's answer — 'The Internet' — is technically correct and completely dismissive, killing the conversation in one word
jokes.explanation: Peak April Ludgate. 'The Internet' is a perfect one-word answer — it's technically helpful, completely dismissive, and shuts down any follow-up. Maximum economy (one word) and extremely high character integration. The fact that it's correct makes it even more devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So what have you been up to?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, I had a cyst removed from my ovary last week, and the doctor said it was the size of a grapefruit. Then I watched six hours of Designing Women in a row.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's... I didn't need to know that.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You asked.

jokes.text: I really like your haircut. Where did you get it? / Prison.
jokes.setup: Chris compliments April's haircut as another small talk attempt
jokes.punchline: April claims she got her haircut in prison — impossible, absurd, and designed purely to end the conversation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Prison' is the perfect escalation from 'The Internet' — it's more absurd, impossible, and conversation-ending. The structure of the bit (Chris asking cheerful questions, April answering in single words that destroy the conversation) is escalating beautifully. 'Prison' earns its own impact because it's specific, unexpected, and perfectly deadpan. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: If you were stranded on a desert island, what's one thing you'd bring?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A boat.

jokes.text: How is your sister doing? She has the shingles. / Who is your favorite character on Sex and the City? / ALF.
jokes.setup: Chris continues his small talk attempts with increasingly bizarre questions
jokes.punchline: April's answer to 'favorite character on Sex and the City' is 'ALF' — a non-sequitur from a completely different era and genre, the furthest possible answer from any actual SATC character
jokes.explanation: The escalation peaks here. 'ALF' as the answer to 'favorite Sex and the City character' is a masterpiece of absurdist comedy. It works on multiple levels: it's from a completely different show, a completely different era, a completely different genre, and it's technically not a human character. April would unironically say this. The specificity of ALF vs. any other random answer is what makes it exceptional. This is the best joke in the Chris/April small-talk sequence and among the best in the episode. Earns 8.8 in craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you mean crazy-eyed? I'm not crazy-eyed!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, in the poll, 34% of respondents described you as 'crazy-eyed.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Crazy-eyed?! I have very sane eyes! These are the eyes of a rational woman!

jokes.text: And nine seconds with Ron. / You're stranded on a desert island, what is the one thing that you bring with you? / Silence.
jokes.setup: Chris reports his progress with Ron; then demonstrates with the classic desert island question
jokes.punchline: Ron answers 'Silence' — both a meta-answer (silence IS what he wants) and a literal shutdown of the conversation
jokes.explanation: The peak of the Chris/Ron/April small talk sequence. 'Silence' is the single best answer to a desert island question ever given on this show. It's simultaneously the thing Ron most wants (to be left alone), the thing that ends this conversation, and a perfect expression of his philosophy. The meta-quality (answering 'what would you bring?' with 'the very thing you are denying me right now') is exquisite. Near-perfect character integration and economy. This and 'ALF' are the episode's standout comedy moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have to go to Eagleton. Eagleton! Do you know what Eagleton is? It's the worst place in the world. It's a suburban hellhole full of snobs and idiots and people who don't appreciate parks or nature or anything good. And I have to go there. Me! Leslie Knope! I have to set foot in Eagleton!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is worse than that time I had to work with Tammy Two. At least Tammy Two is just one person. Eagleton is like a thousand Tammy Twos in khakis.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And if I have to make a movie about this experience, it's going to be called 'Eagleton 2: The Wrath of Khan.' Wait, no. 'Die Hard: With a Vengeance in Eagleton.' Actually, 'Eagleton Forever: The Reckoning.' No! 'Eagleton: The Squeakquel.'

jokes.text: 13% think I'm crazy-eyed? What? Why?
jokes.setup: A flash poll shows 68% of people think Leslie is lying; she processes the numbers
jokes.punchline: Leslie ignores the damaging 68% figure and fixates on the 13% 'crazy-eyed' result — a perfect Leslie priority mis-calibration
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie character beat. She completely skips over the existential threat (68% think she's lying) to address the vanity issue (13% think she's crazy-eyed). This is a perfect encapsulation of how her mind works — and the confused 'What? Why?' is the ideal follow-up. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Alexis
dialogue.line: Hey Leslie! How are you doing today?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you want?

jokes.text: God, don't make me go to Eagleton. Eagleton is the land of rich, snobby jerks. There's a whole chapter about it in my book. I could write a second book about Eagleton and how stupid it is. And I'd call it, Eagleton: The Land of Rich, Snobby Jerks.
jokes.setup: Leslie is told she needs to go to Eagleton to get her original birth certificate
jokes.punchline: Leslie's hatred of Eagleton escalates from complaint to hypothetical book pitch — and the hypothetical book title is identical to her complaint, showing zero creativity in her rage
jokes.explanation: A wonderful Leslie escalation. Her Pawnee chauvinism is a core character trait and watching it expand into a second book proposal where the title is literally just her complaint restated is very funny. The self-awareness gap (she thinks this is a great title) is perfect Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'd like to get a table for two without a reservation.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, sir, we're completely booked.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Oh, I think you'll find we can make this work. I'm Chris Traeger, Deputy Director of the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: And I think you'll find we can't.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: But... I'm extremely likable.

jokes.text: Take it down a notch, Alexis. I need a copy of my birth certificate.
jokes.setup: The Eagleton county records clerk, Alexis, greets Leslie with excessive enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate command to 'take it down a notch' reveals that even enthusiasm from Eagletonians is intolerable to her
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat. Leslie being hostile to even basic Eagleton friendliness is a good joke, and 'Take it down a notch, Alexis' has good snap to it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna break into the records office.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna break something.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Probably me.

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Chris. I was wondering if you might make an exception for me. / Oh, I'm sorry. No. / Wow. That usually works.
jokes.setup: The clerk won't make an exception for the birth certificate; Chris steps in to charm her
jokes.punchline: The charm fails completely; Chris's stunned 'Wow. That usually works.' reveals he is accustomed to effortless success through sheer charisma
jokes.explanation: A very good Chris Traeger joke. His superhuman positivity usually bends reality to his will, so encountering someone immune to his charm completely floors him. 'Wow. That usually works.' is delivered with genuine, childlike confusion — not arrogance. Highly quotable outside context.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: The infantilizing language and pet names

jokes.text: That's broken. [The door Andy attempts to enter through is broken/blocked]
jokes.setup: Andy dramatically attempts to enter the records office for his 'mission'
jokes.punchline: His dramatic entry is immediately foiled — the door doesn't work, deflating the whole moment
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy deflation — the big dramatic moment immediately undercut by mundane reality. Works for the Andy character and gets a solid laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know, Star Trek is actually quite fascinating from a philosophical standpoint. The Prime Directive raises interesting questions about cultural intervention and—wait, sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm being a nerd.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But seriously, the original series had incredible storytelling, and the way they used science fiction to explore real social issues was revolutionary. Did you know that the first interracial kiss on television was between Kirk and Uhura? That was groundbreaking!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And don't even get me started on the technical specifications of the Enterprise. The warp core, the dilithium crystals—it's all so elegant in its design. I could talk about this for hours.

jokes.text: Hold on. Leslie, real quick. Spell your last name for me.
jokes.setup: Andy is in the middle of his 'mission' to get Leslie's birth certificate
jokes.punchline: The implication that Andy has forgotten how to spell Leslie's last name mid-mission — despite presumably needing to fill out paperwork — reveals the depth of his incompetence
jokes.explanation: A great Andy joke. The implication of having forgotten — or never having known — how to spell the last name of his boss and friend is perfectly timed. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Take me home, dumpling. It's beddy time.
jokes.setup: Joan is heavily intoxicated after lunch
jokes.punchline: Drunk Joan using 'dumpling' as an endearment and 'beddy time' as a phrase is an absurd infantilization from someone who was recently presenting herself as a sophisticated sexual being
jokes.explanation: A strong character reversal joke. Joan who was the peacock/sexual predator is now saying 'beddy time' like a toddler. 'Dumpling' is a funny specific word choice. Good escalation of Joan's drunk arc.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm shutting down Grawndy's. I know it's my dream, but... Leslie needs me right now. And that's more important.

jokes.text: They're making a sequel. I'm assuming with the same alternate timeline. But if J.J. Abrams and company expect us to believe that it's Spock with the romantic tension with Uhura and not Kirk, well, let's just say the message boards are going nuts.
jokes.setup: Tom instructs Ben to talk about 'nerd stuff' to cool down Joan
jokes.punchline: Ben delivers a genuine and passionate opinion about Star Trek fandom — 'let's just say the message boards are going nuts' — with total earnestness while Tom is in crisis
jokes.explanation: Ben's nerd monologue is funny because he's completely sincere — this is a real opinion he holds. 'The message boards are going nuts' as an authority citation is peak Ben. Strong character integration — only Ben Wyatt cites message board consensus as evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wow, this Egyptian cotton is incredible. Feel this.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, focus. We need to get Joan to bed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I am focused. I'm focused on the thread count. This is 1,200 thread count, Ben. Do you know what that means?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It means you need to stop touching the sheets and help me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It means I've been living a lie, Ben. A lie of substandard bedding.

jokes.text: I want to take you both home and...bend you over and just...at the same time.
jokes.setup: Ben is mid-Star Trek speech; Joan is extremely drunk
jokes.punchline: Joan interrupts Ben's boring speech with a deeply inappropriate and specific sexual proposition — with the pauses making it worse
jokes.explanation: High impact because of context and delivery — the pauses implied in the transcript ('and...bend you over and just...') suggest she's thinking through the logistics of her proposition in real time, which is uniquely disturbing. The interruption of Ben's Star Trek speech makes the tonal whiplash even sharper.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got it! I got the birth certificate!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, that's amazing! How did you manage that?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, I just walked into the records office, found the file, and grabbed it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you just took it?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I may have also taken a briefcase that wasn't mine on the way out.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You stole a briefcase?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't know, it was just sitting there. Seemed important.

jokes.text: I'm leaving. / Let's do this. / We've got to get her home. / Tom, I know your business is failing, but this just isn't worth it. / It's not about the business anymore, man. She's a disaster. We've got to make sure she gets home safe.
jokes.setup: Joan's proposition lands; Ben wants to leave; Tom makes a decision
jokes.punchline: Tom's declaration — 'It's not about the business anymore, man. She's a disaster. We've got to make sure she gets home safe' — is a surprising moment of genuine moral clarity from Tom Haverford
jokes.explanation: A good character moment for Tom — funny because the very person who was willing to use Joan for business is now the voice of moral responsibility. The comedy is in the unexpected role reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, so I wasn't born in Eagleton?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was born in Pawnee? Oh my God, I'm a Pawnee native. I'm basically a traitor to everything I've ever believed in.

jokes.text: Whoa! What the hell? Okay, let's get her on the bed. Okay. One... Oh, my God. Two... Two... Three. Three.
jokes.setup: Ben and Tom try to get the drunk Joan into bed
jokes.punchline: The difficulty of moving Joan — requiring multiple attempts to even count to three — combined with the pained reactions, implies she is either heavier or more unwieldy than expected
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that works in context. The counting stuttering ('Two... Two... Three. Three.') implies the lift was much harder than expected. Functional physical comedy, not exceptional writing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie's Mother
dialogue.line: We were living in Eagleton at the time because of the raccoon infestation in Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mom, there was no raccoon infestation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie's Mother
dialogue.line: That's what we told you.

jokes.text: Say what you will about Joan, but she knows how to decorate a bedroom.
jokes.setup: In the midst of a crisis (getting drunk Joan to bed), Tom pauses to appreciate her bedroom decor
jokes.punchline: Tom's priorities are so perfectly Tom — even in an emergency, he's aesthetically evaluating interior design
jokes.explanation: A good Tom Haverford character beat. The absurdity of complimenting bedroom decor while in a crisis, and framing it as a balanced assessment ('say what you will'), is perfectly Tom. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I feel terrible about misleading all those people. I mean, what I did was really dishonest and unethical, and I just... I can't believe I would do something so wrong. I mean, the only thing worse than what I did would be if I were from...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Eagleton.

jokes.text: Where the hell am I? / I just want to see how soft these sheets are. One second. / Tom. No. Come on. Let's go.
jokes.setup: Joan briefly wakes up, disoriented; Tom takes the opportunity to feel the sheets
jokes.punchline: Tom, while trying to leave, cannot resist feeling the sheets — his aesthetic curiosity overrides urgency again
jokes.explanation: A nice extension of the bedroom appreciation gag. Tom can't help himself — Ben's exasperated 'Tom. No.' has the rhythm of something he says often.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So I was examining this patient and found this huge cyst, and I had to drain it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: How huge? Like a golf ball?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Did it make a sound when you drained it? Like a whoosh?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What color was the fluid?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why are you both so excited about this?

jokes.text: I also got this dude's briefcase. It was just laying there. Kind of a panic move.
jokes.setup: Andy returns triumphant with Leslie's birth certificate
jokes.punchline: Andy has also inexplicably stolen a random person's briefcase — not for any reason, just because it was there and he panicked
jokes.explanation: A great Andy joke. The admission 'Kind of a panic move' is simultaneously an explanation and a non-explanation — it tells us nothing about why he took it while telling us everything about how Andy's mind works. The specificity of 'this dude's briefcase' and the casual delivery make it land. Earns 8+ through character integration and the perfectly chosen phrase 'panic move.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I did it! I got April and Ron to talk to each other. I am a genius. A beautiful, idiot genius.

jokes.text: Okay, so, Leslie Barbara Knope. Born January 18 to Robert and Marlene Knope in Eagleton, Indiana. / I'm from Eagleton.
jokes.setup: Andy triumphantly reads out the birth certificate
jokes.punchline: The birth certificate confirms Joan's accusation — Leslie WAS born in Eagleton — making Andy's 'Bert Macklin' mission ironically counterproductive
jokes.explanation: A great structural punchline to the A-plot. The mission to prove Leslie's innocence has confirmed her guilt. 'I'm from Eagleton.' delivered with full devastation is the earned payoff of the whole episode's setup. High structural score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no need for small talk. I do not play the game. When someone compliments me, I simply nod once and move on.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's a great strategy, Ron. You're really a man of few words.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: *nods once*

jokes.text: I'm from Eagleton. [long beat of silence/shock]
jokes.setup: Andy has just read that Leslie was born in Eagleton.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's horrified reaction to the discovery — 'I'm from Eagleton' delivered as if it's a terminal diagnosis.
jokes.explanation: The horror-movie delivery of 'I'm from Eagleton' is the emotional peak of the episode's comedy. The joke is entirely in Leslie's face and voice — four words freighted with existential dread. Character integration is nearly perfect: only someone with Leslie's level of Pawnee identity investment would react this way to a county of birth. Earns 8+ for the combination of perfect delivery context, payoff structure, and high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, I know this is hard. Leslie cares deeply about doing the right thing, but sometimes the right thing and the smart thing aren't the same. You have to weigh the consequences. Will telling the truth actually help anyone, or will it just blow everything up? Because if it's the latter, then maybe you sit on it for now.

jokes.text: Pawnee Hospital was overrun with raccoons at the time, so we had to go to the next closest hospital.
jokes.setup: Leslie confronts her mother about being born in Eagleton
jokes.punchline: The reason for the Eagleton birth is that Pawnee Hospital was 'overrun with raccoons' — an insane but completely plausible Pawnee explanation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Overrun with raccoons' as a legitimate medical facility excuse is perfect Pawnee worldbuilding. It's specific enough to be immediately funny (raccoons, not rats or generic vermin) and it's the most Pawnee reason imaginable. The joke also retroactively explains the whole episode's conflict in one absurd sentence. Earns 8+ through originality and world-specific character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You know what, Ben? That's solid advice. I'm going to start calling you by the wrong name.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: From now on, you're Gerald.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My name is Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Not anymore, Gerald.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. Did you expect me to give birth to you in an infested, disease-filled room?
jokes.setup: Leslie is upset that her mom didn't tell her she was born in Eagleton.
jokes.punchline: The mother reframes the question as a reasonable medical choice — which it is — exposing the absurdity of Leslie's priorities.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — the mother is completely reasonable, which makes Leslie's horror more absurd. The specific 'infested, disease-filled room' is funnier than just 'infested room' — the detail compounds the reasonable-ness of the mother's choice.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I apologize for my behavior last night. I must have had some bad seafood.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Joan, we were at Applebee's. You ordered a salad.

jokes.text: You try telling that little girl she's not from Pawnee. I certainly couldn't.
jokes.setup: Leslie's mother explains why she never told Leslie the truth
jokes.punchline: The implication that child Leslie's Pawnee identity was so ferociously established that her own mother couldn't correct it — suggesting Leslie was always exactly this person
jokes.explanation: A warm character joke. The image of a small Leslie Knope being so intensely Pawnee-identified that her mother couldn't bring herself to correct her is both funny and endearing. Strong character integration — it confirms the character's consistency from childhood.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was born at Pawnee General Hospital, which is right next to the old Rubber Nipple factory. My parents actually met at Nipple Hill, which is what we called the hill behind the factory. So yeah, I'm about as Pawnee as they come.

jokes.text: Well, this guy came in. He got his hand stuck in a Pringles can, and he tried to cut himself out. / Was there a lot of blood? What kind of blade did he use? / Three and a half inch. Serrated. Buckets of blood. He passed out over his arm and slumped onto the floor. / Did the bone show?
jokes.setup: Ann starts telling a gross medical story to get the group's attention; April and Ron are immediately rapt
jokes.punchline: April and Ron (who rarely engage with anyone) are suddenly intensely interested, asking follow-up questions with expertise — 'Did the bone show?' from Ron is the peak
jokes.explanation: A great scene that uses character inversion for comedy. April and Ron — who refuse to engage with normal social interaction — are immediately drawn in by medical gore. Ron asking 'Did the bone show?' with the authority of someone who needs this information is perfect. Reveals character through unexpected enthusiasm. Good structure building to the bone question.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jim Boehmer! From Lincoln High! You used to wear those glasses with the tape on them, and you had that weird rash on your neck that you'd scratch until it bled.

dialogue.speaker: Jim
dialogue.line: How do you know that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And you were allergic to dairy, but you'd eat it anyway because you wanted to impress that girl Jennifer, and then you'd have to go to the nurse's office and get your stomach pumped.

dialogue.speaker: Jim
dialogue.line: Okay, that's enough.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Plus you wore the same pair of khakis three days in a row, and there was that incident in tenth grade where you peed yourself in the cafeteria because you were too shy to ask for the bathroom pass.

jokes.text: Very good question, April. Answer her. / Yeah. The bone showed. / Everyone in the universe loves a gross medical story. Boom! I win!
jokes.setup: April asks about the bone; Ron endorses her question; Ann confirms
jokes.punchline: Chris declares victory — 'Everyone in the universe loves a gross medical story. Boom! I win!' — as if this gross story is his achievement and the key to achieving his small-talk goal
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to Chris's small talk mission. He achieves his goal not through charm or conversation topics, but through a gross medical story — and declares it a victory for his thesis about universal human connection. His triumph is completely unearned and completely sincere. 'Boom! I win!' is very Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I love Pawnee. I love it with all of my heart. It's the most wonderful place in the world. Look, some people love waffles, some people love pancakes. But I love Pawnee. It's like a waffle - golden, crispy on the outside, soft and fluffy on the inside, and it makes you happy.

jokes.text: I forgot about the toe. / So did we. / Crazy, right? / That story's awesome.
jokes.setup: Ann has been telling an escalating gross medical story about a Pringles-can injury; she adds a final element
jokes.punchline: 'I forgot about the toe.' — the story has been so detail-rich that Ann herself forgot a major element (a toe), and the group's honest 'So did we' confirms total audience investment
jokes.explanation: A solid escalation joke. The medical story builds well and the communal 'So did we' for the forgotten toe is a great structural payoff. Ann forgetting her own story's key element implies it's almost too much to keep track of.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I've been fact-checking everything the department says for the last six months.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's great, Jerry. What have you found?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, turns out we don't actually need to fact-check anything. We're the government. Nobody checks us.

jokes.text: Indeed. Thank you for sharing, Jenny. / Ann was getting a little chummy. When people get too chummy with me, I like to call them by the wrong name to let them know I don't really care about them. That's a genius move. / Thank you. / You're welcome, Lester.
jokes.setup: Ron calls Ann 'Jenny' after the medical story; explains this is deliberate
jokes.punchline: Tom calls the wrong-name strategy 'a genius move,' Ron thanks him, then immediately calls Tom 'Lester' — the punchline demonstrates the policy is immediately applied to Tom
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structured jokes. The setup (Ron explains his wrong-name policy), the compliment (Tom calls it genius), the gracious acceptance (Ron says 'thank you'), and then the instant application ('You're welcome, Lester') is a perfect four-beat comedic structure. It's also completely character-specific — only Ron would have this policy and only Ron would apply it so immediately. The structural elegance alone earns high craft scores. This is the best Ron joke in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You know what? Let him be happy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, I agree. It's not hurting anybody.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. I wonder who else was born in Eagleton. / Voldemort, probably.
jokes.setup: The office processes the news that Leslie was born in Eagleton
jokes.punchline: April's immediate association of Eagleton with Voldemort — delivered deadpan as if this is a reasonable and obvious parallel
jokes.explanation: A great April Ludgate one-liner. 'Voldemort, probably.' has maximum economy — two words with a trailing 'probably' that implies she's thought about this and Voldemort is only her most likely guess. The Harry Potter reference works because it's the most evil fictional character and April deploys it with complete seriousness. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: The only thing the voters need to know about you is your name. And even that, I go back and forth on.
jokes.setup: Ron is advising Leslie not to disclose her Eagleton birth, arguing voters don't need to know personal details
jokes.punchline: Ron suggests even knowing a candidate's NAME is questionable — his anti-government, anti-transparency ideology taken to its logical extreme
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron Swanson's philosophy taken to its natural conclusion: voters don't need to know anything about a candidate — not even their name. The build-up ('the only thing...') creates an expectation of a minimum threshold, and then 'And even that, I go back and forth on' annihilates even that minimum. Perfect Ron, maximum economy, highly quotable. Clearly earns 8.7.

jokes.text: Damn it. He's right. Well said. / Thanks, Ron. / You're welcome, Steve.
jokes.setup: Ron makes a heartfelt and correct point about identity being about where you're from, not where you were born; Leslie thanks him
jokes.punchline: Ron responds to Leslie's 'Thanks, Ron' with 'You're welcome, Steve' — calling her the wrong name to signal he doesn't actually care
jokes.explanation: The callback to the 'wrong name' running gag at exactly the right moment. Ron has just given genuinely warm and sage advice to Leslie — and immediately undercuts any sentimentality by calling her Steve. It's structurally perfect: the emotional beat and the comedic deflation happen in the same breath. The choice of 'Steve' (not even close to Leslie) is the right level of absurdity. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Well, that is worse than I ever could have hoped for.
jokes.setup: Leslie publicly admits she was born in Eagleton on Joan's show
jokes.punchline: Joan's reaction — 'worse than I ever could have hoped for' — reveals that Joan's fondest hopes involved Leslie's public humiliation, and reality has exceeded them
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed Joan line. The word 'hoped' — implying she had hopes for Leslie's downfall — and 'worse than I ever could have hoped for' as an expression of glee is perfect character work. The inverted idiom (usually 'better than I hoped') works perfectly. Economical and quotable.

jokes.text: When I was nine years old, I broke my arm sledding on that giant hill behind Kernston's Rubber Nipple factory. You know, Nipple Hill.
jokes.setup: Leslie is making her case for being truly from Pawnee through shared community memories
jokes.punchline: The factory name 'Kernston's Rubber Nipple factory' and the casual local nickname 'Nipple Hill' — delivered without embarrassment as completely normal local geography
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist worldbuilding joke. 'Kernston's Rubber Nipple factory' is a perfect Pawnee-style business name — industrial, specific, and inappropriate. 'Nipple Hill' as the casual local name for the sledding hill is even better. Leslie's complete unselfconsciousness about saying this on live TV is the joke. Earns 8+ through originality and Pawnee-world specificity.

jokes.text: It gets very slippery there. I know that. / Especially when it's wet. Yes.
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions Nipple Hill and Joan — the journalist pursuing a 'gotcha' — responds to demonstrate local knowledge.
jokes.punchline: Joan and Leslie riff sincerely on the properties of Nipple Hill ('gets slippery,' 'especially when wet') during a live news interview.
jokes.explanation: The conversation about Nipple Hill's physical properties ('slippery,' 'especially when wet') on live television is structured beautifully — two people who hate each other momentarily uniting in shared local knowledge of a nipple-named hill. The double entendre is implicit and the show knows it. The shared community knowledge angle also makes Leslie's point about belonging more effectively.

jokes.text: It gets very slippery there. I know that. / Especially when it's wet. Yes.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Joan are discussing Nipple Hill's sledding conditions on live TV
jokes.punchline: Their earnest discussion of Nipple Hill's surface conditions — 'slippery' and 'especially when it's wet' — is inadvertently rife with double entendre, which they're both oblivious to
jokes.explanation: A solid extension of the Nipple Hill joke. The unintentional double entendres pile up naturally — 'slippery,' 'wet' — and the comedy is enhanced by both women being completely oblivious and sincere. Works as a callback and a cringe-double-entendre.

jokes.text: Do you remember when you peed your pants in second grade? Why did you bring that up? I said yes. You stuck your underwear in your drawer and you got real embarrassed, and then the teacher came over and pulled them out? And everybody called you 'the gerbil' because you always smelled like soiled wood chips?
jokes.setup: Leslie is proving her Pawnee roots through shared memories with Joan on live TV
jokes.punchline: Leslie overshares a progressively more humiliating story about Joan's pants-wetting incident — on live television — including the soiled-underwear-drawer detail and the nickname 'the gerbil' because of the wood chip smell
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best extended cringe sequences. Leslie telling Joan's most embarrassing childhood story on live TV to prove she's a local is a perfect escalation. Each detail is worse than the last: the accident itself → hiding the underwear → teacher exposing them → the nickname 'the gerbil' → the explanation 'soiled wood chips.' The nickname is a masterpiece of specific absurdity — gerbils, soiled wood chips, the smell connection. Leslie's total obliviousness to how this sounds makes it even better. High craft and impact.

jokes.text: Leslie, for God's sake. We're on TV.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been publicly humiliating Joan with the gerbil story
jokes.punchline: Joan — who hosts a show defined by public 'Gotcha' humiliation — protests 'We're on TV' as if Leslie is the one being inappropriate
jokes.explanation: A perfect irony beat. Joan's protest is the funniest thing she could say given that she built an entire TV career on public humiliation. The irony is completely earned because we've seen Joan's Gotcha tactics throughout. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Joan put us in her book club. Although I could do without this. [Joan's book club sticker is applied to Leslie's face/something inappropriate]
jokes.setup: The book club sticker achievement is reported
jokes.punchline: Joan has placed the sticker somewhere uncomfortable or inappropriate as a final petty act — Leslie's complaint implies it's somewhere she'd rather it wasn't
jokes.explanation: A nice visual callback to the episode-long sticker subplot. The joke works because it's visually apparent (we can see where Joan put it) but the transcript leaves us to imagine — in context, it's likely on Leslie's face or clothing rather than the book.

jokes.text: Indianapolis, Bloomington, Lafayette, Muncie, Gary, all the places you mention in the book. And I've interviewed all the people you mentioned. And so far, there is not one incorrect fact. So, now, I am going to head to the house, say hey to Gayle, wish my daughter a happy belated birthday, it was yesterday...
jokes.setup: Jerry reports his fact-checking progress (all correct) and then shares his personal plans
jokes.punchline: Jerry casually mentions that his daughter's birthday 'was yesterday' — he's been fact-checking Indiana towns while missing his own daughter's birthday, and he mentions it with complete equanimity
jokes.explanation: A great Jerry joke. Jerry has been out in the field missing his daughter's birthday for Leslie's mission, and he mentions it as a casual 'oh by the way' — his boundless accommodating nature making even this sacrifice seem trivial. 'It was yesterday' delivered without any bitterness is peak Jerry.

jokes.text: Nope. You're doing great. Godspeed. / Doing what I can. Yep. / Got to go, Donna. Can't talk. / He just seems so happy. / I didn't say anything.
jokes.setup: Jerry reports his progress; Leslie knows the truth (she was born in Eagleton) but doesn't tell him; Jerry happily heads back out
jokes.punchline: Jerry leaves cheerfully to continue his mission, completely unaware it's now pointless; 'He just seems so happy' / 'I didn't say anything' is a perfect silent indictment of Leslie's choices
jokes.explanation: A perfect dark comedy ending. Jerry — who missed his daughter's birthday — is being sent back out on a now-pointless mission, and he's happy about it. 'He just seems so happy' from Donna is the right amount of dark, and Leslie's defensive 'I didn't say anything' confirms her guilt. The episode ends on a note of warmth-tinged cruelty that is very Parks & Rec.

jokes.text: He just seems so happy. / I didn't say anything.
jokes.setup: Jerry walks out happily to continue his pointless road trip mission.
jokes.punchline: Donna notes that Jerry 'seems so happy' — his ignorance is bliss — and the colleague's 'I didn't say anything' is a deflection from the guilt of watching him go.
jokes.explanation: The button on the Jerry sequence. 'He just seems so happy' is darkly funny because Jerry's happiness is built on ignorance of his own exploitation. The colleague's defensive 'I didn't say anything' implies an accusation being preemptively deflected. Good final beat for the episode's darkest running joke.

tmdb_overview: Leslie's book about Pawnee comes out just in time for her campaign. Ann tries to bond with Ron and April.
insight: Small-town politics comedy grounds 72 jokes in character dynamics over spectacle.
